stem: A 45-year-old patient with a known history of psoriasis complains of pain and stiffness in the fingers, most pronounced in the morning. The stiffness improves as the day progresses with movement. On examination, mild swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints is noted. Based on the clinical features, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
keywords: History of psoriasis – Strong clue linking joint symptoms to psoriatic arthritis.
DIP joint swelling – Classic site of involvement in psoriatic arthritis (helps distinguish from RA).
Morning stiffness improving with activity – Indicates inflammatory arthritis pattern rather than OA or gout.

C.title: Psoriatic arthritis
C.body:
Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. While it can manifest in several ways (symmetric, asymmetric, or spinal), the involvement of the DIP joints (the joints closest to the fingertips) is a hallmark feature that distinguishes it from Rheumatoid Arthritis.
Patients often experience "morning stiffness" that lasts more than 30 minutes and improves with activity—a sign of inflammatory rather than degenerative pain.
Another key diagnostic feature often seen is "dactylitis" (sausage-like swelling of an entire finger) and nail changes such as pitting or onycholysis, which are present in about 80% of PsA patients.
Can present as asymmetric oligoarthritis, spondyloarthritis, or arthritis mutilans.
This patient’s psoriasis history + DIP involvement + morning stiffness is classic for psoriatic arthritis.

A.title: Osteoarthritis
A.body:
Usually presents with joint pain worsened by activity and relieved by rest, not morning stiffness.
Commonly affects DIP, PIP, and first carpometacarpal joints.
Swelling is usually bony enlargement (Heberden’s nodes) rather than inflammatory swelling.

B.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
B.body:
Typically causes morning stiffness >1 hour that improves with activity.
Symmetric involvement of small joints (MCP, PIP).
DIP joints are usually spared, making it less likely in this patient.

D.title: Septic arthritis
D.body:
Usually acute, severe, and monoarticular with redness, warmth, and systemic signs like fever.
Rarely chronic or mild; patient in question has gradual symptoms, so less likely.

E.title: Gout
E.body:
Typically causes sudden, severe pain in a single joint, often the first MTP (big toe).
Chronic gout can affect multiple joints, but DIP involvement is less common, and morning stiffness pattern is not typical.

keyConcept:
Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis, commonly affecting DIP joints and showing morning stiffness that improves with activity.
Distinguishing features from RA, OA, gout, or septic arthritis are pattern of joint involvement, symmetry, and clinical context.

featureTable.description: Affects 10–30% of patients with psoriasis; can precede or follow skin lesions
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Usually adults, both genders; family history may be positive

featureTable.description: DIP joints, PIP, sometimes MCP, asymmetric oligoarthritis, spine (spondylitis)
featureTable.clinicalImportance: DIP involvement + nail changes suggest psoriatic arthritis

featureTable.description: Morning stiffness improving with activity, pain, swelling, tenderness
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Inflammatory pattern distinguishes from OA (worse with activity)
Helps differentiate from RA and gout

featureTable.description: X-ray: pencil-in-cup deformity, joint erosion; ESR/CRP elevated; RF negative
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Imaging supports diagnosis; labs mainly to rule out other arthritis

featureTable.description: NSAIDs for mild disease, DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine), biologics for severe
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Treatment tailored to severity, joint involvement, and comorbidities

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Symmetric small joint involvement (MCP, PIP), spares DIP, prolonged morning stiffness
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: RF and anti-CCP positive; systemic features common

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Joint pain worsens with activity, improves with rest; bony swelling (Heberden’s nodes)
Acute monoarticular attacks, often first MTP; severe pain, redness
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Urate crystals on synovial fluid;recurrent flares

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Usually post-infection; asymmetric lower limb arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis
Acute, severe, monoarticular pain with swelling,erythema, fever
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Urgent management; synovial fluid culture positive

diagram.name: Psoriatic Arthritis in Psoriasis Patients
diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates the key clinical manifestations of psoriatic arthritis in patients with psoriasis, highlighting inflammatory joint involvement (especially DIP joints), morning stiffness improving with movement, dactylitis (sausage digits), enthesitis, nail changes (pitting and onycholysis), spinal involvement (spondylitis), and characteristic radiological findings such as pencil-in-cup deformity.
